title: Which Way Do You Run Genetics?

scenes.tts: A larva has lost part of its body pattern, but nobody knows the gene. Which end of the problem should we start from? Genetics can run from a visible phenotype toward a gene, or from a chosen gene toward a phenotype.
scenes.narration: A larva has lost part of its body pattern, but nobody knows the gene. Which end of the problem should we start from? Genetics can run from a visible phenotype toward a gene, or from a chosen gene toward a phenotype.

scenes.visual: Build the carried 16:9 world and colour map used by both films. PHENOTYPE or assay readout is GREEN; a chosen GENE is PURPLE; GUIDE is BLUE; Cas9 is GOLD; PAM is ORANGE; uncertain or mixed outcomes are GREY. Everything is a labelled block or cartoon, never a molecular structure. A pale larva fills the centre and slowly crawls; several body bands glow GREEN, while one missing band leaves a gap. A large question mark drifts above the gap. A PURPLE gene card sits blurred behind a frosted panel marked 'unknown'. On the opening question, two broad paths begin growing left and right from the larva. Keep a small 'schematic' label at lower right.
The two paths keep extending as the title 'Which Way Do You Run Genetics?' fades in for two seconds, then dissolves. The larva continues crawling and its green bands pulse gently.

scenes.tts: Keep the laboratory bench in view. On its left, organisms with varied phenotypes move toward an assay gate. On its right, a named gene enters before any phenotype appears. These are not different toolkits. They are different directions of reasoning.

scenes.visual: The larva shrinks into a wide laboratory bench occupying most of the frame. The left lane is labelled 'phenotype first'; pale organisms carrying different GREEN trait badges move rightward toward a large GREEN assay gate. The right lane is labelled 'gene first'; a single PURPLE gene card moves leftward toward a neutral cell cartoon. Curved arrows over both lanes point in opposite directions. Transform the same bench rather than cutting layouts.

scenes.tts: In the phenotype-first lane, random mutations enter before the assay. The gate keeps individuals with the chosen trait. Researchers recover lines, map each lesion, and test a candidate gene. This forward path can uncover genes nobody expected. But only visible outcomes reach the gate.
scenes.narration: In the phenotype-first lane, random mutations enter before the assay. The gate keeps individuals with the chosen trait. Researchers recover lines, map each lesion, and test a candidate gene. This forward path can uncover genes nobody expected. But only visible outcomes reach the gate.

Researchers recover lines, map each lesion, and test a candidate gene. This forward path can uncover genes nobody expected. But only visible outcomes reach the gate.
scenes.visual: Zoom to the left lane. GREY mutation badges drop onto moving organisms before they reach the gate. The gate opens only for a GREEN segmented-pattern badge; selected organisms move into a tray labelled 'recover lines'. Their grey badges converge onto a simple PURPLE chromosome bar, then one candidate gene block rises with a question mark. A separate test arrow loops from the candidate back toward the phenotype without showing a result.

scenes.tts: Now imagine a mutation that changes meiosis but never changes the trait scored at the gate. Will this forward screen recover it? Watch the unaffected-looking individuals pass beyond the assay while the hidden mutation stays inside them.
scenes.narration: Now imagine a mutation that changes meiosis but never changes the trait scored at the gate. Will this forward screen recover it? Watch the unaffected-looking individuals pass beyond the assay while the hidden mutation stays inside them.
scenes.caption: Now imagine a mutation that changes meiosis but never changes the trait scored at the gate. Will this forward screen recover it? Watch the unaffected-looking individuals pass beyond the assay while the hidden mutation stays inside them.
scenes.visual: Keep the same gate. One organism receives a GREY badge labelled 'meiotic change' inside its silhouette, but its outward GREEN trait badge looks ordinary. It approaches the gate and continues toward an unselected exit. Large question text appears above the bench: 'Can the assay select what it never sees?' The hidden badge pulses faintly.

Deliberate thinking pause. Hold 'Can the assay select what it never sees?' The outward trait badge bobs beside the gate while the hidden grey meiotic badge pulses inside the passing organism. No answer appears.

scenes.tts: No. The screen cannot select a difference its assay never records. Forward genetics is open to unexpected mechanisms, yet bounded by phenotype. A different assay might reveal the same mutation. The blind spot belongs to the measurement, not to the gene.

scenes.visual: The question transforms into 'assay blind spot'. A translucent cone of GREEN light projects from the gate and covers only visible trait badges. The organism with the grey hidden badge moves outside that cone. A second gate with a different GREEN symbol slides in briefly; its light reaches the hidden badge, showing that another assay could expose it. Keep both gates labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: In the gene-first lane, begin with a named gene. Lower its output with RNA interference, or alter its D N A with Cas nine. Then measure what changes. This reverse path asks a focused question. It stays silent about genes nobody chose to perturb.
scenes.narration: In the gene-first lane, begin with a named gene. Lower its output with RNA interference, or alter its DNA with Cas9. Then measure what changes. This reverse path asks a focused question. It stays silent about genes nobody chose to perturb.
scenes.caption: In the gene-first lane, begin with a named gene. Lower its output with RNA interference, or alter its DNA with Cas9. Then measure what changes. This reverse path asks a focused question. It stays silent about genes nobody chose to perturb.
scenes.visual: Pan along the same bench to the right lane. A PURPLE gene card enters a cell cartoon. It forks into a BLUE RNA-interference arrow that lowers a protein-output gauge and a GOLD Cas9 block guided toward a PURPLE DNA bar. Both routes end at a row of GREEN phenotype meters. Other grey gene cards remain behind a closed cabinet labelled 'not chosen'.

scenes.tts: The approaches therefore miss different things. Forward screens miss phenotypes outside their assay. Reverse experiments miss genes outside their chosen list. Neither direction turns one changed trait into a complete mechanism. That requires a separate causal test.

scenes.caption: The approaches therefore miss different things. Forward screens miss phenotypes outside their assay. Reverse experiments miss genes outside their chosen list. Neither direction turns one changed trait into a complete mechanism. That requires a separate causal test.
scenes.visual: Pull back to both lanes. Over the forward lane, the green assay cone leaves grey phenotypes outside its edge. Over the reverse lane, one purple gene card is lit while a shelf of other genes stays grey. Both lanes end at candidate cards carrying question marks. A separate neutral test loop grows beside each candidate without showing any specific answer.

scenes.tts: A pooled Cas nine screen combines the directions. Researchers choose many guides gene by gene, then usually give each cell a single guide. A selection keeps cells with a phenotype. Sequencing identifies guides that became enriched or depleted. Those guide counts nominate candidates.
scenes.narration: A pooled Cas9 screen combines the directions. Researchers choose many guides gene by gene, then usually give each cell a single guide. A selection keeps cells with a phenotype. Sequencing identifies guides that became enriched or depleted. Those guide counts nominate candidates.
scenes.caption: A pooled Cas9 screen combines the directions. Researchers choose many guides gene by gene, then usually give each cell a single guide. A selection keeps cells with a phenotype. Sequencing identifies guides that became enriched or depleted. Those guide counts nominate candidates.
scenes.visual: The two lanes bend together into one loop. Several BLUE guide cards, each paired with a different PURPLE gene label, shuffle into separate cells. Most cells visibly receive one blue card; no percentages appear. A GREEN selection gate keeps a subset. Their blue guide cards rise into two animated bar groups labelled 'enriched' and 'depleted', then transform into candidate cards with question marks.

scenes.tts: Follow the bench from question to claim. A phenotype-first screen may discover an unimagined gene. A gene-first experiment may test a precise hypothesis. A pooled screen may survey many chosen genes together. In every case, the assay defines what becomes visible.
scenes.narration: Follow the bench from question to claim. A phenotype-first screen may discover an unimagined gene. A gene-first experiment may test a precise hypothesis. A pooled screen may survey many chosen genes together. In every case, the assay defines what becomes visible.
scenes.caption: Follow the bench from question to claim. A phenotype-first screen may discover an unimagined gene. A gene-first experiment may test a precise hypothesis. A pooled screen may survey many chosen genes together. In every case, the assay defines what becomes visible.
scenes.visual: Three compact routes animate across the same bench, one after another: GREEN phenotype to PURPLE gene; PURPLE gene to GREEN phenotype; many BLUE guides through a GREEN selection gate. Each route ends at a candidate card, not a verdict. A movable GREEN spotlight sweeps across each route and illuminates only the outcomes its assay can see.

scenes.tts: So ask these questions before interpreting any genetic result. What did the experiment choose first? What could its assay actually detect? Those questions reveal both its reach and its blind spot. The direction is part of the evidence.

scenes.visual: The bench simplifies into two large moving arrows. The GREEN phenotype-first arrow travels toward a PURPLE gene card; the PURPLE gene-first arrow travels toward a GREEN phenotype card. A small assay spotlight travels with each arrow and leaves a soft grey shadow outside its view. The two question prompts appear in turn, then fade before the end card.

Clear everything to one centred line only: 'What you choose first determines what a genetic experiment can find.' No title, logo, subtitle, or smaller line. A faint green-to-purple arrow moves slowly behind the words without adding another mark.
